interviewQuestions.question: Why does narrating your thought process matter as much as writing correct code?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because the interviewer can only score what they can observe, and reasoning that stays in your head is invisible to them - correct or not.

Two candidates can produce identical working code and leave with very different scores: one talked through the approach, its complexity, and a mid-solution course correction the whole way; the other went silent for five minutes and typed out a finished answer. The interviewer credits the first candidate's thinking directly. For the second, they can only infer it from the final artifact, and they have no way to tell a genuine insight from a lucky guess or a memorized solution.

Narration also captures partial credit that silence throws away. If you're 80% of the way to a correct approach when time runs out, saying so out loud - "I think sorting first gets me most of the way, I just haven't worked out the edge case" - gets scored as real progress. The same 80%, held silently, gets scored as failure.

The practical loop I use is: state the approach, state its complexity, then start typing - and repeat that loop every time the plan changes, rather than silently revising and hoping the final code speaks for itself.

**Testing:** whether you understand that an interview measures observable reasoning, not just output.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: How do you decide how much to narrate, so you're neither silent nor drowning the interviewer in commentary?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I narrate decisions and their reasons, and let mechanical code speak for itself.

A decision is anything where a different answer would change the code: choosing a hash map over sorting, picking recursion over iteration, deciding an edge case needs its own branch. Those get a sentence each, because the reasoning behind them is exactly what the interviewer can't see just by reading the result. A `for` loop incrementing an index, or a variable being assigned zero, doesn't need narration - describing every line in full sentences buries the one decision that mattered under ten that didn't, and reads as filler rather than clarity.

Early in the interview I narrate more generously, because the interviewer is still building a model of how I think and every stated trade-off adds signal. As I'm implementing a plan we've already agreed on, I let the narration compress - a short status ping like "handling the base case, then recursing" is enough, since re-explaining an already-understood plan every ten seconds adds nothing.

The one place I never let narration compress is when I'm privately reconsidering the whole approach - that's exactly the moment to say so out loud, because silence there is indistinguishable from being stuck.

**Testing:** whether you can calibrate narration density rather than defaulting to one extreme.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Judgement

interviewQuestions.question: Should you always mention the brute-force approach before presenting an optimal solution, even when you see the optimal one immediately?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Yes, briefly - even a one-sentence mention, because it's the cheapest way to show the interviewer you understood the trade-off rather than pattern-matched to an answer.

Saying "the obvious approach is checking every pair, O(n squared); I can do better with a hash set, one pass, O(n)" costs about ten seconds. Without it, a candidate who derived the optimal solution by genuinely reasoning through the naive one first looks identical to a candidate who recognized the problem shape and recalled the answer from memory - the code is the same either way, and the interviewer has no way to distinguish the two unless the baseline is stated.

The exception is when the brute force is genuinely not obvious or would take real time to explain and isn't adding anything - in that case I'll still name the complexity I'm targeting and why, even without walking through a slower alternative in detail: "I'm going straight to a two-pointer approach here since the array's sorted; the naive version would be O(n squared), this gets it to O(n)."

What I avoid is silently jumping to the optimal solution with zero acknowledgment that a slower approach exists - that's the version that reads as memorized rather than reasoned, regardless of how correct the final code is.

**Testing:** whether you understand that naming a baseline is what turns a correct answer into demonstrated reasoning.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: You're thirty seconds into total silence while coding and realize you've actually hit a dead end with your current approach. What do you say, and why does that moment matter more than the earlier narration did?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I stop and say it directly: "actually, this approach breaks on duplicate keys - let me back up and reconsider." That single sentence matters more than almost any other narration in the interview, because it's the moment where silence and stalling become genuinely indistinguishable from the interviewer's side.

Earlier silence, while implementing an agreed, well-understood plan, is low-risk - the interviewer already has the mental model and doesn't need it restated every few seconds. But silence at the exact moment you've privately discovered your plan doesn't work is the highest-risk kind, because from outside it looks identical to being stuck with no idea what to do next. The interviewer can't tell "reconsidering deliberately" from "lost" unless you say which one it is.

Naming the specific failure - not just "this isn't working" but "this breaks on duplicate keys" - also converts a stall into a checkpoint: it shows the interviewer you have a concrete, falsifiable reason for changing direction, and gives them a natural point to either let you self-correct or nudge you toward the fix.

The broader principle: the value of narration isn't constant throughout the interview - it's highest at exactly the moments where staying silent would be misread as failure rather than reflection.

**Testing:** whether you recognize that narration timing matters as much as narration content, especially at points of genuine uncertainty.
